title: Ikhfāʾ shafawī — hiding the meem at the lips
objectives: Student can identify a meem sākinah followed by ب on sight, and can say why the sequence only ever occurs across a word boundary.
Student can produce the light-contact lip posture — touching, not sealing — and can feel the difference between it and a fully closed meem.
Student can hold the 2-count ghunnah behind the lips before releasing the ب, without either pressing shut or opening early.
Student can read تَرْمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٍ correctly cold, from her own memorised al-Fīl.

slides.heading: Lesson 3.15 — Ikhfāʾ shafawī: the lips touch but do not press
Read this one phrase. You know it by heart.
body: تَرْمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٍ — al-Fīl 105:4. Read it before anything is explained.

One of two things almost certainly happened. Either the lips pressed shut and produced a clean tarmīhim, then biḥijāratin — two separate words with a full stop between them. Or the meem vanished altogether: tarmīhi-bḥijāratin.
Both are wrong, and the sentence is this: the lips are supposed to be somewhere in between, and stay there for two counts.
Brought together so lightly they are barely touching. The nasal runs behind them for a slow two. Only then does the ب pop open.
Name the error before it happens, because it will: you will press. Every language you speak presses its m. Two counts of light contact is not a sound you have ever needed before today.

audio.cue: 105:4 — lips barely touching, nasal running for two counts behind them, then the ب released. Put a finger against your own lips: they are together, and nothing is being pressed.

slides.heading: The whole chapter, in thirty seconds
body: A meem sākinah has exactly three possible futures, decided entirely by the next letter.
ب — concealed, lips lightly touching, 2-count ghunnah. That is today.
م — merged into one doubled meem, 2-count ghunnah. That is 3-17.
Any of the other 26 letters — said plainly, lips fully closed, no hold. That is 3-18.
Two exceptions and a default. Draw it once and leave it on the board for four lessons. You should never be wondering how large this chapter is.

slides.heading: What you already have
body: 3-15 gave you the nasal itself and the two-count hold. Today's rule is that same hold, in a new place — behind lips that are not shut. You already own the sound; today it moves.
2-03 gave sukūn: a closed letter, said with no vowel after it. A meem sākinah is exactly that, and the whole meem chapter is about what happens to a closed meem depending on what stands beside it.
2-05 taught that a shadda's first half IS a sukūn. You have been producing closed meems since then without a name for the situation.
From Unit 2 you already read أَلَمْ تَرَ and لَكُمْ دِينُكُمْ correctly by instinct. Those are the OTHER meem rule, and you are right about them. The name arrives in 3-18.

slides.heading: Ikhfāʾ shafawī — labial concealment
slides.condition: A meem sākinah (مْ) followed by ب. In the Qurʾān this only ever happens across a word boundary.
body: The meem is concealed — ikhfāʾ — with a 2-count ghunnah, lips lightly touching and never sealed.

Shafawī means labial, 'of the lips', from شَفَة. It is named that way against the other ikhfāʾ you meet in 3-24, al-ikhfāʾ al-ḥaqīqī, the 'true' concealment, which hides a NOON and happens on the tongue. Same operation, different letter, different place in the mouth.

The condition has a structural fact worth pointing at: مْ + ب always occurs across two words, and the sequence never arises inside a single word. The meem is always the last letter of its word and the ب always opens the next one. You never have to check mid-word for this rule, and that is true without exception.
One letter triggers it. There is no list to memorise.

slides.heading: Teach the posture with your hand, not with words
body: Hold a fingertip lightly against your closed lips and try three things in sequence.
PRESS — say a hard m. You feel the pressure on your finger. That is a doubled meem, not today's rule.
OPEN — say b with no meem at all. No contact.
TOUCH — bring the lips together until they are just in contact, hum, and hold. Almost no pressure on the finger. The third is the rule.
The diagnostic, said out loud every time: if you can feel your lips tense, you are pressing.

Then add the timing. Lips in the light-contact position, ghunnah for two counts on the fingers exactly as in 3-15, and only when the second finger lands does the ب release. The commonest execution fault is a correct posture held for half a count.

audio.cue: PRESSED — a doubled meem. Real pressure on the fingertip. Not today's rule.
OPEN then POPPED — a bāʾ with no meem in front of it. Closed, then released.
TOUCHING — barely in contact, humming for two counts. This is the target, and it is the row you must be able to hit on purpose rather than by luck.

slides.translation: Striking them with stones of baked clay.

audio.cue: 105:4 — the single in-set instance, and the ayah keeps giving. تَرْمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٍ is today's rule; three words later بِحِجَارَةٍ مِّن سِجِّيلٍ is a merge with ghunnah, which is 3-21. One ayah, two lip-and-nasal rules, already in her memory. Do not go looking for a better example; there isn't one.

slides.heading: One ayah, two rules — and one preview of a third

pairs.note: Today. A meem sākinah before ب: lips lightly touching, 2-count ghunnah, then the ب released.
Three words later in the same ayah. A tanwīn merging into a م — same 2-count nasal, but the lips close and two letters become one. Its lesson is 3-21.

Reference example — outside your memorised sūrahs. A NOON turning into a concealed meem, then four letters later a MEEM being concealed. The mouth does the same thing twice, from two different written letters. Its lesson is 3-23.

slides.heading: The forward pointer that will save a whole lesson later
body: In seven lessons you meet iqlāb, where a NOON before ب becomes a concealed meem. The lip posture is identical and the sound is nearly indistinguishable.
The two rules differ only in what was written before the rule applied: a م (today) or a ن (3-23).
This is said now, in one sentence, and said again then. Learners who meet the two rules cold, weeks apart, file them as one rule with a naming problem.

And the boundary in the other direction: in 3-18 you will be told that a meem before any OTHER letter has its lips FULLY closed and no hold. Ikhfāʾ shafawī before ب — lightly touching, 2 counts. Iẓhār shafawī before the other 26 — fully closed, not prolonged. These two are lip-posture opposites and they differ by one letter.

slides.heading: One disagreement, stated once and not drilled
body: A minority of scholars hold that a meem sākinah before ب is iẓhār, not ikhfāʾ — their reasoning being that the meem and the ب already share the lips, so there is nothing to hide.
The jumhūr position is ikhfāʾ, and this course teaches ikhfāʾ.
It is mentioned in one sentence so that if you hear a teacher press the lips fully on تَرْمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٍ you recognise a known disagreement rather than concluding you were taught wrongly.
Practically the two positions differ by very little: how much contact and how much hold, not whether a meem is there at all.

slides.heading: A rare rule, and therefore a rare colour
The finger test, three postures
slides.instructions: Fingertip resting against your lips. Say each one and report what you felt. Repeat until you can hit the middle row on purpose rather than by luck. Once, on day two, do this in front of a mirror: you should be able to SEE your lips together and SEE that they are not compressed.

audio.cue: PRESSED. Real pressure on the fingertip — this is a doubled meem, not today's rule.
BARELY TOUCHING. Almost no pressure. If you can feel your lips tense, you are pressing.
CLOSED THEN POPPED. A bāʾ with nothing in front of it.

slides.heading: Build it from the pieces
slides.instructions: Say the left of each pair with a deliberate gap, then the right joined. The left column is deliberately wrong — say it anyway, because it makes the join audible.

audio.cue: WRONG on purpose — two words, a full stop between them, lips pressed shut on the meem.
105:4 — right. Light contact, two counts, then the ب. No breath and no pause at the boundary.
WRONG on purpose — apart.
2:8 — reference example, outside your memorised sūrahs. A clean single instance with nothing else in the way.
WRONG on purpose — apart.
2:33 — reference example, outside your memorised sūrahs. Two lip-nasal rules four letters apart, and the mouth does the same thing in both.

slides.heading: Two counts behind the lips
slides.instructions: Fold two fingers during the hold. Do not release the ب until the second finger has landed. Then do each one wrong on purpose — release after one count — so you can hear what you are avoiding.

audio.cue: 105:4 — the hum runs behind closed-but-untensed lips for the whole two counts. Finish the hum, THEN open.
2:8 — reference example. Two counts, then the ب comes out clean and un-muffled.
2:33 — reference example. Two counts on the second of the two lip-nasals; the first belongs to 3-23.

slides.heading: Is it a ب, or not?
slides.instructions: Read each pair. The first of each pair is today's rule; the second is not. Say the label before you read. Make yourself name the letter that follows the meem — the rule is decided by that letter and by nothing else.

audio.cue: TODAY — ب follows. Lightly touching, two counts.
NOT TODAY — 105:1, ت follows. Lips fully shut, no hold. Same sūrah, three words in.
TODAY — ب follows.
NOT TODAY — 109:6, د follows. Lips shut, released clean.
TODAY — ب follows.
NOT TODAY — 105:3, ط follows. Lips shut, no hold, and the meem stays light despite the heavy letter.

slides.heading: In the sūrah, whole
slides.instructions: Recite al-Fīl from memory, all five ayat, at your normal pace. The rule has to survive being surrounded by other words. If it only works when you are looking at it, it is not learned yet.

grid.arabic: أَلَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِأَصْحَٰبِ ٱلْفِيلِ
grid.translit: alam tara kayfa faʿala rabbuka bi-aṣḥābi-l-fīl

audio.cue: 105:1 — أَلَمْ تَرَ. Lips shut, no hold. Establish the contrast at the start of the sūrah.
105:3 — عَلَيْهِمْ طَيْرًا. Shut again, and the meem does not thicken before the heavy ط.
105:4 — today's rule, then a merge with ghunnah three words later. Two lip-and-nasal operations in one line, and both hold for two.

slides.heading: The six things that go wrong

mistakes.wrong: Pressing the lips shut — a clean, fully-formed meem, tarmīhim, with a real stop before the ب.
mistakes.why: Every language she speaks has a pressed m and none has a lightly-held one. This is the default, not carelessness. It sounds tidy, which is why it survives.
mistakes.fix: Fingertip on the lips. 'Less. Again. Less.' Do not explain; adjust by feel.

mistakes.wrong: Leaving the lips apart — no meem at all: tarmīhi-bḥijārah.
mistakes.why: Over-correction. 'Do not press' is heard as 'do not close'. It usually appears the moment error one is fixed.
mistakes.fix: 'Touch. Not press, not open — touch.' Back to the three-posture drill, in order.

mistakes.wrong: Omitting the ghunnah — the posture is right and the release is immediate.
mistakes.why: The posture is the new and interesting part, so all the attention goes there and the timing is dropped. Very common in the same session the posture is fixed.
mistakes.fix: Fingers. Two folds, then release. Do not let her run the phrase without them until day three.

mistakes.wrong: Applying it to a meem before something other than ب — a soft, held meem in أَلَمْ تَرَ or لَكُمْ دِينُكُمْ.
mistakes.why: New rules over-apply for about a week. Expected, not alarming.
mistakes.fix: 'What letter comes next?' Make her name it. The rule is decided by that letter and by nothing else.

mistakes.wrong: Breaking the two words apart — a micro-pause between تَرْمِيهِم and بِحِجَارَةٍ, sometimes a breath.
mistakes.why: It is a word boundary, and Unit 2 trained her to read words as units. The rule requires the join.
mistakes.fix: Build-from-pieces, left column then right, twice. Then the whole ayah in one breath.

mistakes.wrong: Nasalising the ب — the hum continuing through the release, so the ب comes out muffled.
mistakes.why: She has learned to stop the nasal and open the lips as one movement, instead of stopping the nasal THEN opening.
mistakes.fix: 'Finish the hum. Then open.' Two separate instructions, deliberately separated in time, then gradually brought back together.

audio.cue: CONCEAL — مْ then ب. Lips lightly touching, 2 counts, then release. 105:4, the only in-set instance.
SAY IT — مْ then ت. Lips fully closed, no hold. Its name arrives in 3-18.
MERGE — a tanwīn into a م. Same 2-count nasal, lips closed, two letters becoming one. Lesson 3-21.
Reference example. Iqlāb, then today's rule. Same posture twice, from a noon and then from a meem. Lesson 3-23.

slides.heading: Homework — 15–20 min/day, five days
tasks: One minute — the finger test, three postures. Every day, first thing, before anything else.
Three minutes — build from pieces, then two counts on the fingers behind the lips.
Two minutes — is it a ب or not. Say the label before each phrase. If you hesitate, mark it.
Three minutes — al-Fīl from memory, whole, at pace.
Once, on day two — the three postures in front of a mirror. Thirty seconds, and it settles the posture question for good.
The rest — hifz. Manzil, Sabqi (al-Falaq 113 and al-Ikhlāṣ 112:1–2), then the new Sabaq al-Ikhlāṣ 112:3–4 from the page.
Bring to the next session: al-Fīl recited from memory, and tell me BEFORE you start where the one ikhfāʾ shafawī is. If you can name it before reciting it, you have it.

BARELY TOUCHING — the target. Lips tense means pressing.
CLOSED THEN POPPED.

drills.title: Build it from the pieces
drills.instructions: Apart first, deliberately wrong; then joined with two counts of light contact.

audio.cue: Wrong on purpose — a full stop between the words.
105:4 — right. Light contact, two counts, no breath at the boundary.
Wrong on purpose.
2:8 — reference example, outside your memorised sūrahs.
Wrong on purpose.
2:33 — reference example. Two lip-nasal rules, four letters apart.

NOT TODAY — ت. Lips shut, no hold.
TODAY — ب.
NOT TODAY — د.
TODAY — ب.
NOT TODAY — ط. And the meem stays light.

drills.title: al-Fīl, whole
drills.instructions: From memory, all five ayat, at normal pace. Name where the ikhfāʾ shafawī is before you start.

audio.cue: 105:1 — lips shut on أَلَمْ.
105:3 — shut again, and light.
105:4 — the one instance, then a merge three words later.

script: Write تَرْمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٍ and ask her to read it. She knows the ayah by heart. She will either press the lips shut and produce two separate words, or lose the meem altogether. Both are wrong; say the one sentence that fixes both: 'the lips are supposed to be somewhere in between, and stay there for two counts.'

Demonstrate it exaggerated: lips barely touching, the nasal running behind them for a slow two, then the ب popping open. Have her put a finger against her own lips while you do it again — she should SEE that they are together and HEAR that nothing is being pressed.
Name the priority error out loud now, because it will happen: she will press. Every language she speaks presses its m. Two counts of light contact is not a sound she has ever needed before today.

Frame the whole chapter in thirty seconds — ب conceal, م merge, the other 26 say plainly. Draw it once and leave it on the board for four lessons. She should never be wondering how large this chapter is.
State the naming: shafawī means labial, from شَفَة, and it is named that way against al-ikhfāʾ al-ḥaqīqī in 3-24, which hides a NOON on the tongue. Same operation, different letter, different place.
Give the structural fact: مْ + ب always occurs across two words and never inside one. That is one less thing to scan for, and it is true without exception.

Teach the posture with her hand, not with words. Press, open, touch — in that order, fingertip on the lips. The third is the rule. Say the diagnostic aloud: 'if you can feel your lips tense, you are pressing.'
Then add the timing, and do not let her release early. A correct posture held for half a count is the commonest execution fault.

Flag the 3-18 boundary now, briefly, so the contrast is expected rather than confusing: ikhfāʾ shafawī has the lips lightly touching for 2 counts, iẓhār shafawī has them fully closed and not prolonged. Lip-posture opposites, one letter apart.

Flag the difference of opinion once and do not drill it. A minority read a meem before ب as iẓhār; the jumhūr and this course read it as ikhfāʾ. Say it so that if she hears a teacher press the lips fully on 105:4 she recognises a known disagreement rather than concluding she was taught wrongly.

Spend your time on 105:4. It is the single in-set instance and the ayah keeps giving: three words later it hands you بِحِجَارَةٍ مِّن سِجِّيلٍ, a merge with ghunnah from 3-21. One ayah, two lip-and-nasal rules, already in her memory. Do not go looking for a better example; there isn't one.

Put 105:1 and 105:4 side by side — أَلَمْ تَرَ presses shut, تَرْمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٍ does not, and both are in one short sūrah she recites from memory. The difference is the single letter that follows, and nothing else.

2:33 contains an iqlāb and then, four letters later, an ikhfāʾ shafawī: the mouth does the same thing twice from two different written letters. Save it for 3-23 if you want the drama, or use it today as a preview. Either works — do not use it both times as though it were new.

The forward pointer that saves a lesson later: in 3-23 a NOON before ب becomes a concealed meem, with an identical posture and a nearly indistinguishable sound. Say it now in one sentence and say it again then. Learners who meet the two cold, weeks apart, file them as one rule with a naming problem.

Hifz: Manzil, then Sabqi (113, plus 112:1–2 — recheck the two-shaddas-no-ghunnah ayah cold; it is exactly the kind of thing that decays in a week), then the new Sabaq 112:3–4. That portion has THREE meem sākinahs — لَمْ, وَلَمْ, وَلَمْ — and not one of them is today's rule, because each is followed by ي. Have her read the portion and count the closed meems out loud. Learning to see a rule and correctly conclude 'not this one' is half the skill.

Note the أَحَدٌۢ at the end of 112:4, with its small standing meem. She has read that mark for years. It is an iqlāb sign and it belongs to 3-23 — if she asks, say 'seven lessons away, and yes, it is related to what we did today.'

listenFor.item: Lips in light contact — together, but with almost no pressure on a fingertip held against them.
listenFor.makhraj: The two lips, brought to contact without compression. The nasal runs from the khayshum behind them while the mouth is closed but untensed.
listenFor.commonMistake: Pressing the lips shut, producing a clean fully-formed meem with a real stop before the ب.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Every language she speaks has a pressed m and none has a lightly-held one. It sounds tidy, which is why it survives correction. This is the default, not carelessness.
listenFor.correctionCue: Fingertip on the lips. 'Less. Again. Less.' Do not explain; adjust by feel.

listenFor.item: A meem that is actually there — the mouth closing, not merely approaching.
listenFor.commonMistake: Leaving the lips apart, so the meem vanishes: tarmīhi-bḥijārah.
listenFor.whyItHappens: Over-correction of pressing. 'Do not press' is heard as 'do not close'. It usually appears the moment the first error is fixed.
listenFor.correctionCue: 'Touch. Not press, not open — touch.' Back to the three-posture drill, in order.

listenFor.item: Two full counts of nasal behind the lips before the ب is released.
listenFor.commonMistake: A correct-looking mouth that releases straight into the ب, with no hold at all.
listenFor.whyItHappens: The posture is the new and interesting part, so all the attention goes there and the timing is dropped. Very common in the same session the posture is fixed.
listenFor.correctionCue: Fingers. Two folds, then release. Do not let her run the phrase without them until day three of the homework.

listenFor.item: The rule applied only where a ب follows — أَلَمْ تَرَ and لَكُمْ دِينُكُمْ still fully closed and unheld.
listenFor.commonMistake: A soft, held meem before letters other than ب.
listenFor.whyItHappens: New rules over-apply for about a week. Expected, not alarming.
listenFor.correctionCue: 'What letter comes next?' Make her name it out loud. The rule is decided by that letter and by nothing else.

listenFor.item: The two words joined — no micro-pause and no breath between تَرْمِيهِم and بِحِجَارَةٍ.
listenFor.commonMistake: Breaking the boundary, sometimes with an audible breath.
listenFor.whyItHappens: It is a word boundary, and Unit 2 trained her to read words as units. The rule requires the join, and مْ + ب only ever occurs across a boundary — so the join is not optional here, it is the rule.
listenFor.correctionCue: Build-from-pieces, left column then right, twice. Then the whole ayah in one breath.

listenFor.item: A clean, un-muffled ب at the release — the hum finished before the lips open.
listenFor.commonMistake: Nasalising the ب, so the hum continues through the release.
listenFor.whyItHappens: She has learned to stop the nasal and open the lips as one movement, instead of stopping the nasal and then opening.
listenFor.correctionCue: 'Finish the hum. Then open.' Two separate instructions, deliberately separated in time, then gradually brought back together.

teacherNotes.homework: 15–20 min/day, five days. Daily: one minute of the three-posture finger test, first thing; three minutes of build-from-pieces then two counts on the fingers behind the lips; two minutes of 'is it a ب or not' with the label said before each phrase; three minutes of al-Fīl from memory, whole, at pace. Once, on day two: the three postures in front of a mirror — thirty seconds, and it settles the posture question for good. Hifz: Manzil, Sabqi (113 plus 112:1–2, with the two-shaddas-no-ghunnah ayah rechecked cold), then the new Sabaq 112:3–4 from the page, counting the three closed meems out loud and confirming that none of them is today's rule. She brings to the next session al-Fīl recited from memory, having named where the one ikhfāʾ shafawī is BEFORE she starts.
